place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育场 · 九月二十四日

setup.zh: 补测。看台上马小宝脚边一箱蛋白粉，赌的是他第七。到六百米，胸口发紧，越吸不进越慌。
setup.en: The retest. On the stand, a case of protein powder at Ma Xiaobao's feet, bet on him coming seventh. At six hundred metres his chest tightens; the less he can draw in, the more he panics.

recap.zh: 补测四分二十九，七人第三；后半程，他在吐气。
recap.en: The retest in 4′29″, third of seven; over the second half he was breathing out.

en: At six hundred, his chest tightens.

story.zh:
九月二十四日，下午四点。补测七个人。看台第三排，马小宝脚边真放着一箱蛋白粉，箱子上拿马克笔写着两个大字：「第七」。他冲沈芒举了举摇杯。

两百米标杆底下站着那件蓝马甲，膝盖上摊着本子。沈芒站在起跑线上，手心里全是汗，两条腿有点发软，昨天肋下那根针好像还在里头等着他。他把眼睛从看台上挪开，只看跑道。

哨子一响，另外六个人冲了出去。那股劲又上来了，心先快，腿先热，人便觉得自己什么都干得成；他咬着牙硬让腿慢下来，一个人落在最后。看台上有人笑出了声，有人喊：「跑啊，阿甘！」他觉得那个举手机的镜头正对着他的后背，觉得那箱「第七」正在他身后笑。他把这两样都塞到脑后头，只听自己的脚步：两步吐，两步吸，用肚子，不用肩膀。

两百米标杆底下，蓝马甲报了一声：「四十六！」慢了一秒。他心里一松：慢一秒，比快十秒强。

到四百米，前头有两个掉了下来，嗓子眼里那种又快又浅的喘，跟他上回一样。他从他们身边过去了。到六百米，他也难受了：腿里那股酸从腿肚子往上爬，胸口发紧，越吸不进越慌，越慌越想快快地吸——
story.en:
September 24th, four in the afternoon. Seven in the retest. In the third row of the stand, at Ma Xiaobao's feet, there really was a case of protein powder, two big characters on it in marker: "SEVENTH". He raised his shaker to Shen Mang.

Under the two-hundred-metre post stood the blue vest, notebook open on her knees. Shen Mang stood on the line with his palms wet and his legs a little soft; yesterday's needle under his ribs seemed still to be waiting for him. He took his eyes off the stand and looked only at the track.

At the whistle the other six shot off. The old surge rose in him — heart first, then hot legs, the feeling that he could do anything — and he clenched his teeth and made his legs slow down, falling in alone at the back. Someone in the stand laughed; someone shouted: "Run, Forrest!" He felt the phone camera trained on his back, felt that case of "SEVENTH" laughing behind him. He shoved both to the back of his head and listened only to his feet: two steps out, two steps in, belly, not shoulders.

Under the two-hundred post the blue vest called: "Forty-six!" A second slow. Something in him eased: a second slow beats ten seconds fast.

At four hundred, two of those ahead fell back, that fast shallow gasping in their throats just like his last time. He passed them. At six hundred it got hard for him too: the ache climbing from his calves, the chest tightening, the less air got in the more he panicked, the more he panicked the faster he wanted to gulp —

exits.means: breathes out first and finishes the retest

refuse.en: Still running. Out first, then in.

story.zh:
先吐。

「呵——」长长地，吐到肚子都瘪了。吐干净了，那一口新气自己灌了进来，一直灌到肚子底下。再吐，再进来。胸口那块石头，松了一点。

最后三百米，他又超了一个人，又一个。最后一百米，他把剩下的力气全掏了出来，两条腿乱蹬，嘴里还在吐气，吐得像一辆上坡的拖拉机。

「沈芒，四分二十九。」雷老师又看了一眼表，「……过了。」

沈芒没蹲，自己往前走，绕着弯道走了半圈。他等着胃里那阵翻江倒海，没有来。他张开嘴，只吐出一口长长的热气。

「成了！」

他喊得太响，看台上那个举手机的人吓了一跳，手机差点掉了。

阿禾把本子转过来，只给他看一行：「9/24　补测　4′29″　七人第三　奖：免账」。那十四天的鸡蛋钱，一笔勾了。「前两百米，比表上慢了一秒。慢得好。」她顿了顿，「后半程，你在吐气。谁教的？」

他想说是一个唐朝的人，又想起来不是唐朝：「……一个记错朝代的老太太。」

她看了他一眼，没问下去，在本子上又记了一笔。

看台上，马小宝拿脚尖把那箱蛋白粉往栏杆边上一推，冲着跑道喊了一嗓子：「七个里第三。运气。」阿禾没抬头，在本子上又添了一笔，道：「后四百米，七人第一。」

沈芒站在跑道上，胸口一起一伏，热得发烫。他没去看那箱蛋白粉，也没去看看台——他看着两百米标杆底下那个低着头的马尾辫，看了足足两秒，才低下头去系鞋带。鞋带没开。

十点，他妈打来视频：「补测怎么样？」「过了。」他妈不说话，先在家长群里翻了半天，才道：「这回没视频。那是真过了。」隔了一会儿，「国庆回来不？车票买了没？」

沈芒张了张嘴：「……还没买。」

夜里，两条腿开始造反了，不是疼，是酸，从脚底一直酸到大腿根。上铺的老蔡听他翻来覆去，从床底下拖出一只泡脚桶——他奶奶寄的，带加热，桶沿上一块小屏幕——往下一递：「借你。我奶奶说，腿酸了，热水一泡，比什么都强。」眼镜从抽屉里摸出一包东西往桶里一倒：「我妈塞的花椒。好不好使不知道，反正香。」沈芒把两只脚伸进去，「嘶——」地一声又缩了回来。眼镜瞅了一眼桶沿那块屏幕：「五十八度。老蔡，你奶奶那是烫猪蹄。」他按灭了加热，拎起桌上那瓶凉白开往里兑了半瓶。沈芒再把脚放进去。这回是热，不是烫；那股酸被热水一捂，一点一点地化开了。他坐在床沿上，看着那一桶浮着几粒花椒的水，心里头有一块地方，暖暖的，不是水烫的。

那夜他睡不着，摸过眼镜桌上那本《抱朴子》，书签夹在讲喘气的一页：拿一根鸿毛搁在鼻口上头，吐气，毛不许动。

他从老蔡枕头的拉链缝里捏出一根细绒毛，搁在鼻子底下，屏住了，慢慢地，慢慢地，往外吐——

毛飞了。

先吐，他是学会了；吐得那么轻、那么长，还差得远——手札里那个老头，鹅毛也飞了一冬天。那根绒毛在路灯光里打了个转，越过墙上那幅节气挂图，越过那张白的一面朝外的卷子，从没关严的窗缝里飘了出去——那扇窗朝着西北——飘进了九月的夜里，不见了。
story.en:
Out first.

"Haaa —" long, until his belly was flat. Emptied, the fresh breath poured in by itself, all the way to the bottom of his belly. Out again; in again. The stone on his chest loosened a little.

In the last three hundred he passed one more, then another. In the final hundred he dug out everything he had left, legs flailing, still breathing out, breathing out like a tractor going uphill.

"Shen Mang, four twenty-nine." Mr Lei looked at the watch again. "...Pass."

Shen Mang didn't squat; he walked on by himself, half a lap round the bend. He waited for his stomach to heave. It didn't. He opened his mouth and only a long hot breath came out.

"Done!"

He shouted it so loud that the one holding up a phone in the stand jumped and nearly dropped it.

Ahe turned the notebook round to show him a single line: "9/24  retest  4′29″  3rd of 7  prize: account waived." Fourteen days of eggs, struck through with one stroke. "First two hundred, a second slower than the chart. Good slow." She paused. "The second half, you were breathing out. Who taught you?"

He wanted to say a Tang dynasty man, then remembered it wasn't Tang: "...An old lady who gets her dynasties wrong."

She gave him a look, didn't ask further, and wrote another line.

In the stand Ma Xiaobao toed the case of protein powder towards the railing and shouted at the track: "Third of seven. Luck." Ahe didn't look up; she added one more line and said: "Last four hundred, first of seven."

Shen Mang stood on the track with his chest heaving, hot through. He didn't look at the case, didn't look at the stand — he looked at the ponytail bent over the notebook under the two-hundred post, for a full two seconds, before he bent to tie his shoe. The lace wasn't undone.

At ten his mother video-called: "How was the retest?" "Passed." She said nothing, scrolled through the parents' group for a while first, then: "No video this time. So you really passed." After a pause: "Coming home for National Day? Bought your ticket?"

Shen Mang opened his mouth: "...Not yet."

That night his legs mutinied — not pain, an ache from the soles of his feet to the tops of his thighs. Old Cai heard him tossing and dragged a foot-bath out from under the bunk — his grandmother had sent it, heated, a little screen on the rim — and handed it down: "Borrow it. My grandma says nothing beats hot water for sore legs." Glasses fished a packet from a drawer and tipped it in: "Sichuan pepper. My mum packed it. No idea if it works, but it smells good." Shen Mang put both feet in — "sssss!" — and pulled them straight out. Glasses glanced at the screen on the rim: "Fifty-eight degrees. Old Cai, your grandma scalds pigs' trotters at that." He switched the heater off and poured half a bottle of cold water in. Shen Mang put his feet back. This time it was hot, not scalding; the ache melted a little at a time in the heat. He sat on the edge of the bed looking at the tub with its few peppercorns floating, and there was a warm place inside him that the water had nothing to do with.

He couldn't sleep, and reached for the Baopuzi on Glasses's desk, bookmark at the page on breathing: lay a goose feather over the nose and mouth, breathe out, and the feather must not move.

He plucked a fine down feather from the open zip of Old Cai's pillow, laid it under his nose, held still, and breathed out slowly, slowly —

The feather flew.

Out first, he had learned; out that lightly, that long, he was nowhere near — the old man in the notes had a goose feather flying all winter too. The down turned once in the streetlight, drifted over the solar-terms chart on the wall, over the sheet pinned blank side out, and out through the window that didn't quite shut — the window facing north-west — into the September night, and was gone.
